https://baltic-review.com/tartu-meeting-.text: Share Tweet 0 Rural energy initiatives are being examined as part of an international meeting in Tartu. From energy idea to local practice Estonia is hosting a timely international discussion about one of the most practical questions in the clean-energy transition: how can rural communities move from individual renewable-energy projects to locally organised systems that deliver lasting benefits? The question is at the centre of the EC4RURAL project’s annual meeting in Tartu on 23–24 September 2026. The gathering brings together project partners working with rural municipalities and communities in Estonia and Galicia, Spain. According to the project announcement by the Galician Federation of Municipalities and Provinces, the meeting is being used to compare pilot experiences, identify obstacles and discuss how local energy communities can remain active beyond the initial project period. The event is taking place as Estonia’s own debate about community energy becomes more concrete. The University of Tartu and the Estonian University of Life Sciences recently hosted a separate conference on 22 September focused on how solar-energy communities can move from an idea to an operating model. That conference presented practical tools for assessing feasibility, financing and cooperation between local authorities, residents, apartment associations, businesses and researchers. Why rural communities matter Energy communities are designed to give local people a more active role in renewable-energy production and use. They can bring together households, companies, municipalities or civic organisations around solar installations, storage, energy efficiency or local energy planning. In rural areas, the model can connect energy policy with wider questions of development. A village may be interested not only in producing electricity, but also in lowering the cost of operating a community building, supporting local businesses, improving the energy performance of homes or retaining more value within the local economy. The EC4RURAL meeting reflects that broader approach. The project’s Estonian partners include the University of Tartu, the Estonian Association of Cities and Municipalities, the Tartu Regional Energy Agency and the Estonian Leader Union. The University of Tartu’s project information says the work is intended to strengthen relationships between municipalities and rural communities while ensuring that less-developed and peripheral areas can participate in the energy transition. Learning from local pilots The Tartu programme includes an exchange of experience between Estonian and Galician pilot areas. It also includes a technical visit to Põltsamaa, where participants are examining local renewable-energy initiatives, the Umbusi community and the work of the Jõgevamaa Cooperation Centre, which supports measures designed to reduce energy costs. That emphasis on visiting operating or emerging initiatives is important. Community energy is often discussed through national targets and large infrastructure, but its success also depends on smaller decisions: who owns an installation, who can use the electricity, how costs are shared, and whether local residents have enough information to take part. Recent reporting by Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR has highlighted the same practical dimension. Participants in a 22 September conference in Tartu described local energy communities as responses to specific needs, such as high electricity costs or the desire to make better use of locally generated solar power. The report also noted that communities continue to face regulatory and technical barriers, including restrictions on sharing surplus electricity through the grid. A constructive test for the transition The Tartu meeting is therefore less about presenting a single universal model than about testing what can work in different places. Rural communities vary in population, infrastructure, income and access to technical expertise. A solution suitable for a village in southern Estonia may need to be adapted elsewhere. That flexibility is also the project’s constructive contribution. By combining municipal knowledge, research, community experience and European cooperation, EC4RURAL is treating the energy transition as a social and organisational process as well as a technological one. The meeting’s second day is dedicated to future planning, project indicators, resources and the continuation of results. For Estonia, the significance lies in whether the lessons gathered in Tartu can help more communities evaluate realistic projects, avoid unnecessary complexity and develop renewable energy around local priorities. Community energy will not replace national grids or larger renewable projects. It can, however, give rural residents a clearer role in the transition and help connect climate goals with everyday concerns such as household bills, local services and regional resilience. https://www.dw.com/en/trump-s-diesel-dea.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OF6H Diesel supplies are under pressure and analysts are skeptical Trump's diesel deal with Russia will lower prices Image: Patrick T. Fallon/AFP Advertisement With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon. That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin . "The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne. The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said. Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined." Wars reducing refinery output Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler. But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war. Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars. "If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said. Trump expects prices to fall at record speed In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel. He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps. Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets." Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel. Diesel — Made in the USA But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on. Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky. Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home. The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports. At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries. Debates over export restrictions continue Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan. "There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again." Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions . "An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski. "Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added. Limited impact on US diesel demand Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact. According to calculations by the platform The World Data , the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels. Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand. "I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement. Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added. Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor. Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute , analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cmx280.text: Watch: Block of flats destroyed in Russian strikes on Ukraine Watch: Block of flats destroyed in Russian strikes on Ukraine Close A key energy facility and a residential building in the outskirts of Kyiv have been hit by overnight Russian missile and drone strikes. In the capital, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said. At least 600,000 people across the country are without electricity after strikes hit critical infrastructure in the Kyiv region and the north-eastern city of Kharkiv. The strikes come after US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine. Russia's defence ministry said its "massive" strikes had targeted communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. BBC Ukraine Correspondent Dan Johnson explains.
